Blasting
BLAST-ing
noun
From the Saxon blaest, a blowing or gust of wind; hence the scorching of standing corn by a hot, withering wind — in the Hebrew shiddaphon, the blight of the east wind that shrivels the ear before it fills.

Biblical Definition

Blasting is the scorching of the standing grain by a burning wind, so that the ear withers in the field before the sickle can be put to it. In Scripture it is never a bare accident of weather. It stands at the head of the covenant sanctions God swore against a disobedient Israel: “The LORD shall smite thee with a consumption, and with a fever, and with an inflammation, and with an extreme burning, and with the sword, and with blasting, and with mildew” (Deu 28:22). The LORD claims the stroke as His own doing. Pharaoh saw it in his dream, where seven thin ears “blasted with the east wind” devoured the seven good ears (Gen 41:6), and Joseph read it as the word of God shewing to Pharaoh what He was about to do. Solomon, dedicating the temple, foresaw the day when blasting would drive Israel to her knees and asked that the prayer made toward that house be heard (1Ki 8:37). Amos names the purpose plainly: “I have smitten you with blasting and mildew … yet have ye not returned unto me, saith the LORD” (Amo 4:9), and Haggai repeats it over a people who panelled their own houses while the LORD’s lay waste (Hag 2:17). Blasting, then, is a rod in a Father’s hand: a withered harvest sent to make a hard people ask why, and to send them home.

Webster 1828 Definition

The scorching or blighting of grain by a hot wind; in Scripture a covenant judgment sent from the LORD’s own hand to summon a people to repentance.

expand to see more

BLASTING, the act of blighting or withering; the destruction of corn or fruit by a scorching wind, mildew, or sudden heat.

From the Saxon blaest, a blast or gust of wind, and thence the injury such a wind inflicts upon growing grain.

Hebrew shiddaphon, from a root signifying to scorch; the east wind of Gen 41:6 that shrivelled the ears.

Ranked in Deu 28:22 among the covenant curses, and in 1Ki 8:37 among the calamities that send Israel to prayer.

Amo 4:9 and Hag 2:17 attribute blasting directly to the LORD as a chastening stroke.

Key Scripture

Deu 28:22 — "The LORD shall smite thee with a consumption, and with a fever, and with an inflammation, and with an extreme burning, and with the sword, and with blasting, and with mildew; and they shall pursue thee until thou perish."

Gen 41:6 — "And, behold, seven thin ears and blasted with the east wind sprung up after them."

Amo 4:9 — "I have smitten you with blasting and mildew: when your gardens and your vineyards and your fig trees and your olive trees increased, the palmerworm devoured them: yet have ye not returned unto me, saith the LORD."

Hag 2:17 — "I smote you with blasting and with mildew and with hail in all the labours of your hands; yet ye turned not to me, saith the LORD."

Modern Corruption

The covenant sanctions upon the field are read either as ancient weather-superstition to be pitied, or their moral weight is transferred whole to a secular dread of the earth’s ruin — a substitute doctrine of last things with no Judge, no sin, and no Redeemer.

expand to see more

Two errors face each other across this word, and both empty it. The first says that Deu 28:22 is the guesswork of a pre-scientific people who blamed their gods for the weather; now that we understand fungus and wind, the theology may be quietly retired. But the passage does not offer a mechanism, it names an Agent: the LORD shall smite thee. Scripture nowhere denies second causes — there really was an east wind in Pharaoh’s Egypt — it denies that second causes are the last word. God governs the wind He made, and He governed it against a covenant people for a declared reason. The second error keeps the dread and discards the Judge. Where men no longer believe that a holy God visits sin upon a nation’s harvest, the fear of ruined fields does not disappear; it is transferred to a doctrine of last things without repentance, in which the earth is the offended party, guilt is measured by consumption rather than by God’s law, and the remedy is policy rather than a Mediator. That is not stewardship; it is the shape of religion poured into a mould that has no God in it. The Christian is bound to till and keep the ground faithfully (Gen 2:15) and to deal honestly with what he is given — and to refuse the counterfeit judgment day.

Recover what Scripture actually says about the ground. It is cursed for man’s sake (Gen 3:17), and the whole creation “groaneth and travaileth in pain together until now” (Rom 8:22), waiting not for a policy but for the manifestation of the sons of God. That groaning is real, and blight is one of its voices. Yet over the same ground stands an oath the flood could not break: “While the earth remaineth, seedtime and harvest, and cold and heat, and summer and winter, and day and night shall not cease” (Gen 8:22). The believer therefore holds two things at once without panic: the field is under the curse and will sometimes wither, and the world will not slip out of the hands that hold it. Blasting is not the end of the world; it is a summons. Amos gives the refrain that interprets every failed harvest in redemptive history — yet have ye not returned unto me. The blighted ear is God’s question, and the only sufficient answer is repentance, faith in Christ, and the prayer Solomon asked God to hear when the corn failed.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

A scorching wind upon the standing corn; in covenant terms, the LORD’s own stroke upon a nation’s bread to bring it back to Him.

expand to see more

Blasting — Saxon blaest, a gust or blast of wind; the blight such a wind works upon grain.

Hebrew shiddaphon, scorching; twinned in every occurrence with yeraqon, mildew.

Five appearances only: Deu 28:22; 1Ki 8:37; 2Ch 6:28; Amo 4:9; Hag 2:17 — all covenantal.

Gen 41:6 supplies the picture: ears “blasted with the east wind” in Pharaoh’s dream.

In Amos and Haggai the LORD speaks in the first person: I have smitten, I smote.

Usage

"Blasting is never bare weather in Scripture — the LORD says I smote you, and means it."

"Deu 28 lists it among the sanctions; Solomon’s prayer treats it as a call to the house of God."

"Amos’s refrain is the point of the rod: yet have ye not returned unto me."
